title: How much is it?
goal: Count, ask prices, and set up Slovak's most surprising number rule: from five upward, the noun changes its form.
bekal: say the numbers 0 to 1,000 and read prices in euros
choose the right noun form after 1, after 2-4, and after 5 and up
ask prices and haggle politely at the market

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na trhu
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning at the Miletičova market in Bratislava. Budi is shopping for fruit on his own for the first time.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Good morning. How much are the apples?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Yes. How much is that wine?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: To je trochu drahé. Máte lacnejšie?
lines.id: That's a bit expensive. Do you have anything cheaper?
lines.literal: that is a-little expensive. you-have cheaper?

lines.speaker: Predavačka:
lines.text: Toto stojí päť eur. Je tiež dobré.
lines.id: This one is five euros. It's good too.
lines.literal: this it-stands five euros-gen. it-is also good.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Dobre, beriem ho. Koľko to je spolu?
lines.id: OK, I'll take it. How much is that altogether?
lines.literal: good, I-take it. how-much that is together?

lines.speaker: Predavačka:
lines.id: Nine euros. Do you have the exact change?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bohužiaľ nie. Mám len dvadsať eur.
lines.id: I'm afraid not. I only have twenty euros.
lines.literal: unfortunately not. I-have only twenty euros-gen.

notes: **Koľko stojí?** literally "how much does it stand?" — Slovak uses *stáť* (to stand) for prices, just like German *kosten* and Russian *стоить*. If what you're asking about is plural, the verb is plural too: *koľko **stoja** jablká?*

**Dve eurá but sedem eur.** This is the heart of this unit. After the numbers 2, 3, 4 the noun takes the ordinary plural (*eurá*); after 5 and up it takes the **genitive plural** (*eur*). Slovak does this with every noun, no exceptions, for life.

**Dve, not dva.** The number two follows gender: *dva* for masculine (*dva stoly*), *dve* for feminine and neuter (*dve kávy*, *dve piva*). The numbers 3 and 4 don't care — *tri, štyri* for everything. So only one number needs attention.

**Nech sa páči** is a ready-made phrase meaning "here you are" when handing something over, "come in" when inviting someone inside, or "have a seat". Literally "may it please you". You'll hear it a dozen times a day.
**Beriem ho** — *ho* stands for *víno*. Notice that *víno* is neuter, and the neuter object pronoun is the same as the masculine one: *ho*.

grammars.title: Numbers and the noun after them — three groups
body: This rule has no equivalent in English, and it applies in every sentence that contains a number. Luckily there are only three groups.
after: **Compound numbers follow their last part?** Not quite — Slovak says *dvadsaťjeden rokov* with the genitive, because compound numbers above twenty always take the genitive plural. For A1, hold on to this simple rule: **every number from five up takes the genitive plural**, including those ending in 1, 2, 3, or 4 inside a bigger number.

**Why does this exist?** It's a leftover from the time when Slavic languages had a special form for "two things". The numbers 2, 3, 4 inherited that form, while 5 and up were once treated as nouns in their own right — "five of tables". The genitive ending is the trace of that long-lost "of".

**The verb follows too.** *Dve kávy **stoja** štyri eurá* (plural), but *Päť káv **stojí** desať eur* (singular). After five, the noun is grammatically no longer a plural subject, so the verb goes back to the singular. It's subtle and beginners often ignore it — get it right and native speakers will notice at once.

grammars.title: The genitive plural: an ending that often disappears
body: The form numbers from 5 up demand. What confuses beginners: for two of the three genders, the ending is not added but **dropped** — and a vowel inside the word often lengthens instead.
after: **The vowel lengthening has rules of its own**, and it looks odd until you see the pattern: *e → ie* (*žena → žien*), *o → ô* (*škola → škôl*), *a → á* (*auto → áut*), *i → í* (*kniha → kníh*). The last vowel of the stem lengthens to make up for the missing ending.
**Words whose vowel is already long don't change**, because the rhythm rule forbids two longs side by side — and because there's nothing left to lengthen: *káva → káv*, *práca → prác*.

**For A1, learn the seven most frequent forms** and let the rest come slowly: *eur, centov, rokov, ľudí, detí, korún, kíl*. Those seven words cover almost every sentence with a number you'll say in your first month.

blocks.text: Notice the pattern that saves a lot of memorizing: **11-19 = unit + -násť** (like English *-teen*), and **20-90 = unit + -dsať or -desiat** (like *-ty*). Once you know 1 to 10, the rest is practically guessable. Only two break the pattern: *štrnásť* (14, not *štyrinásť*) and *pätnásť* (15, with *ä*).

Compound numbers are joined without spaces or linking words: *dvadsaťjeden* (21), *tridsaťpäť* (35), *stodvadsať* (120), *tisícdeväťstodeväťdesiatosem* (1998). That monster really is written as one word — which is why Slovaks themselves prefer to write it in figures.

blocks.title: Štrnásť: a small, useful drill
items: *Štrnásť* (14) has no vowel in its first syllable: *št-r-násť*, said *SHTR-nahst*. It belongs with *štvrtok* (Thursday) and *štvrť* (quarter).
If you can say all three smoothly, you've cleared most of the sound hurdles Slovak has.

blocks.text: Slovakia has used the euro since 2009. Its noun forms follow the number rule above, which makes it perfect daily practice.

Notice that Slovak writes prices with a **decimal comma** and the € sign after the number. And **the word *cent* is dropped** when it follows an amount in euros: *dve eurá päťdesiat*, not *dve eurá päťdesiat centov* — just as English speakers say "two fifty". The word *cent* is used in full only when there are no euros at all.

blocks.title: The koruna still alive in people's mouths
items: Before the euro, Slovakia's currency was the *slovenská koruna* (Sk). It was worth about 30 korunas to the euro.

Twenty years after the switch, older people still often count in korunas in their heads, and sometimes say it out loud at the market. If you hear a number that sounds thirty times too big, that's why.
